extracted.intended_audience: general readers; journalists, researchers, and fact-checkers tracking corporate disinformation
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia list article cataloging websites created by companies that have been identified by journalists, fact-checkers, or researchers as distributing false news or participating in misinformation/disinformation. Entries show site name, domain, status, notes and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The following is a list of websites that have been created by companies and have been considered by journalists, fact-checkers or researchers as distributing false news - or otherwise participating in misinformation or disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sentence defines why a site appears on the list: it must be company-created and have been identified by third-party journalists/fact-checkers/researchers as distributing false or misleading content. The article notes the list is dynamic and may be incomplete; additions should be sourced to reliable outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership / funding disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites created or funded by companies that do not adequately disclose ownership or funding on articles or site pages (e.g., 'Does not disclose its ownership on articles', 'funded and fully owned by Chevron', 'funding disclaimer appears on the homepage, but not on articles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pages highlight non-disclosure or partial disclosure as a red flag (examples: Alabama News Center, Richmond Standard, Permian Proud). Guidance implicitly used by the article: lack of clear ownership/funding attribution supports classification as corporate disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation / impostor sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that imitate established news outlets' branding or present themselves as another outlet (e.g., 'Imitated CNN.com, complete with the CNN logo', 'Impostor site of BBC News', 'Impostor site of CNBC').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonation—using logos, similar domain names, or copycat layouts—is cited as evidence of deceptive intent and a reason for inclusion (examples: cnn-trending.com, bbcnewstoday.com, cnbcnewstoday.com).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of specific misinformation topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites repeatedly promoting demonstrably false or misleading narratives on particular topics (examples from the page: 'Promoted climate change denialism', 'repeatedly made false claims about COVID-19', 'shared COVID-19 misinformation and false information about elections').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article groups and flags sites by the kinds of misinformation they spread (climate denial, COVID-19, election misinformation, etc.), using third‑party reporting to substantiate those claims (e.g., GB News, thefederalistpapers.org).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pink-slime journalism / content-farm characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites or networks described as 'pink slime' or content farms—low-cost, factory-produced outlets that publish syndicated or low-quality articles and may spread sanctioned or propagandistic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes descriptions such as 'pink slime' and cites investigations (e.g., Big News Network, content farms impersonating outlets). These features are treated as markers of coordinated, low-transparency operations rather than independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republishing PR / press releases as news
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that republish corporate press releases or PR material presented as news (e.g., 'Many articles on its website appeared to be a corporate press release', 'Republishes press releases from Chevron in Spanish').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republishing company materials without clear labeling or critical reporting is used as evidence the site functions as corporate propaganda (examples: Permian Proud, Juicio Crudo, El Oriente, Richmond Standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden bylines / ghost authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are hidden or not credited properly (e.g., 'Author bylines are hidden in the website source code', 'does not include the names of local reporters', 'author worked at a public relations firm').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden or misleading author attribution—especially where authors have PR affiliations—is presented as an indicator of deceptive practice and reduces the outlet's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting news deserts / creating 'news mirages'
rubrics_metrics.description: Company-run sites that present as local news in areas with 'little-to-no news coverage' or that create a 'news mirage'—local-sounding outlets that advance a corporate agenda in underserved regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites investigations noting these outlets exploit gaps in local reporting to disseminate corporate-friendly content (examples: Permian Basin coverage, Richmond Standard). This pattern is a rationale for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal / regulatory enforcement as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites or operators subject to legal action or enforcement (e.g., 'the Federal Trade Commission...filed complaints against several dietary supplement marketers accusing them of creating fake news websites').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC complaints, court rulings, or other enforcement actions are used as authoritative evidence that a website network engaged in deceptive or fraudulent practices (examples: Beony International, LeanSpa, Sensa and associated domains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation-management firms operating site networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks of sites created by reputation-management or PR firms for influence or damage-control purposes (e.g., 'sites created by Eliminalia, a reputation management firm', followed by a long list of domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a single firm producing many localized or themed sites is treated as a pattern of coordinated reputation management rather than independent journalism (Eliminalia list is given as an explicit example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in scams or deceptive commercial schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites used in support of scams or deceptive commercial operations (e.g., pushing the 'Hawking Code' scam; content used by betting company Jackpot Bet Online; fake news websites used to advertise weight-loss products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Banc de Binary / cnn-trending.com, jackpot-bet associated sites, FTC actions against weight-loss marketers) show how fake-news sites can be part of direct consumer deception or fraudulent schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as paid marketing / publicity stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake-news or fake-outlet sites created as part of marketing or publicity campaigns (e.g., 'A Hollywood Film Is Funding Fake News As Part Of Its Publicity Campaign').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites instances where entertainment marketing or other campaigns deliberately created deceptive outlets—this commercial motive is a classificatory factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on third-party reporting and fact-checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification and notes are based on being 'noted by' or 'described by' journalists, fact‑checkers, research organizations and watchdogs (examples: The Guardian, NPR, PolitiFact, Gizmodo, NewsGuard, Center for Countering Digital Hate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article’s sourcing column and notes indicate that inclusion depends on external reputable reporting or research; readers should consult cited sources for detailed evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain status labelling (Active / Defunct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each entry includes a 'Status' field indicating whether the domain is 'Active', 'Defunct', or otherwise (examples shown repeatedly in the site tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status helps assess current risk or ongoing activity; defunct domains may be listed for historical record while active domains are current concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlinked networks and cross-linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that link to each other or form visible networks (e.g., 'Links to Juicio Crudo and El Oriente', Amazon Post / El Oriente / Juicio Crudo cross-links).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-linking among sites is presented as evidence of coordinated network behavior and can be used to trace corporate information campaigns.
